hints.junior: Every click on a page actually happens twice: once walking down to what you clicked, once walking back up. addEventListener only listens to the walk up, by default.
hints.mid: A bubble-phase listener (the addEventListener default) can be silenced by an inner element's stopPropagation() before it ever runs. A capture-phase listener can't — it already ran on the way down.
hints.staff: This is why real 'click outside to close' implementations register on document with { capture: true }, not the bubble-phase default most code reaches for without thinking about it.

hints.junior: Click Inner in both modes and watch the log. Same click, opposite order: bubble goes Inner-Middle-Outer, capture goes Outer-Middle-Inner.
hints.mid: event.eventPhase in the log confirms this isn't just call-order — capture-phase listeners genuinely run in phase 1, bubble-phase in phase 3, reported by the browser itself.
hints.staff: Toggling only changes the third argument to addEventListener on all three boxes. Nothing else about the click or the DOM structure changes between the two runs.

hints.junior: Think of it as walking down a hallway to a room, then walking back out. addEventListener's third argument picks which trip a listener hears: capture is the walk in, bubble is the walk out.
hints.mid: capture: true attaches a listener to the downward pass instead of the default upward one — the same three-argument addEventListener call, just one option different, and the fire order across nested elements completely reverses.
hints.staff: Capture-then-target-then-bubble is the DOM Events spec's dispatch algorithm, identical across every evergreen browser. event.eventPhase (1/2/3) reports which pass is currently running, independent of any framework.

hints.junior: React's onClick in JSX is always bubble-phase. If you need capture, the prop has a Capture suffix: onClickCapture, onMouseDownCapture, and so on.
hints.mid: { capture: true } composes with { once: true } in the same options object — a common combo for 'run exactly once, before anything downstream can suppress it', like dismissing a tooltip on the next click anywhere.
hints.staff: removeEventListener must match the capture value used at registration or it silently no-ops instead of throwing — the most common real bug with capture-phase listeners, and a genuine leak in components that mount/unmount repeatedly.

anecdotes.junior: I built a dropdown that wouldn't close when you clicked a button inside a totally unrelated widget. That widget's button called stopPropagation() on its own click, and my document-level bubble listener never even fired. Switching my listener to capture: true fixed it in one line.
anecdotes.mid: The bug is invisible in isolation — your dropdown's own tests pass, because nothing inside YOUR component calls stopPropagation(). It only shows up once another team's widget does, on a page you don't control end to end.
anecdotes.staff: This is why component libraries default their outside-click detection to capture: it's defensive against code they don't own and can't audit. If you're shipping a widget other teams will compose with arbitrary other widgets, assume something downstream will call stopPropagation() eventually.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's about a DOM quirk that breaks 'click outside to close' menus in a way that's genuinely confusing to debug — the click happens, your listener just never hears about it.
sections.mid: This case covers event capture vs bubble phase: what addEventListener's third argument actually does, and why real component libraries lean on capture for outside-click detection specifically.
sections.staff: We're covering the DOM Events dispatch algorithm's three phases, the addEventListener capture option, and the removeEventListener capture-matching gotcha that's the most common real bug here.

sections.junior: The concept chapter is the principle. Read it before the demo so the toggle makes sense.
sections.mid: The third argument to addEventListener controls which walk a listener hears — { capture: true } attaches it to the downward pass, omitting it attaches it to the upward pass, the default almost everyone uses without thinking.
sections.staff: This is defined by the DOM Events spec's dispatch algorithm, not a browser quirk — stopPropagation() halts whichever phase is currently in progress, it can't retroactively cancel listeners that already ran in an earlier phase.

sections.junior: Click the small Inner box, watch the fire order in the log, then flip the toggle and click again — same click, reversed order.
sections.mid: event.eventPhase in the log is the browser confirming this for real, not just JS call order looking that way.
sections.staff: Only the capture option on addEventListener changes between the two demo states — everything else about the click is identical.

sections.junior: Capture-then-target-then-bubble is defined by spec, identical across every browser. A capture-phase listener can''t be silenced by an inner element''s stopPropagation — it already ran before that element was even reached.
sections.mid: This is exactly why real "click outside to close" implementations register on document with { capture: true }, not the bubble-phase default — stopPropagation() can't reach back and cancel a listener that already ran.
